words.s: Pardon: dropping a wrong you are owed, without the other person having to earn it.
A contract: a binding agreement formed by an offer and its acceptance.
The part of the body that must be covered, which varies by person and by setting.
The evil eye: real harm that can follow an admiring or an envious look.
The original ruling, before any concession applies: the default rather than the exception.
The waiting period a woman observes after divorce or a husband's death before remarrying.
Self-admiration: being impressed by your own good deed as though you produced it alone.
Local custom, which fiqh accepts as a decider where revelation has left a matter open.
The Prophet's closest friend, his companion in the cave, and the first caliph.
The Companion who narrated more hadith than any other, from about four years in the Prophet's company.
Good manner in a specific situation: the right way to sit, speak, eat, enter, and ask.
The uprightness of a narrator: sane, adult, Muslim, not openly sinful, not known for shameful habits.
The punishment or ease a person meets in the grave, before the Day of Judgement arrives.
The call announcing that a prayer time has entered, given aloud before each obligatory prayer.
The set remembrances of the day: morning, evening, sleeping, waking, eating, travel and distress.
Any hadith that does not reach the level of mutawatir, however strong its single chain may be.
The Prophet's household, honoured by all Muslims, though the schools draw its boundary differently.
People who lived without a prophet's message reaching them, and the question of how they are judged.
The main body of Muslims who follow the Prophet's way and the practice of his companions.
The Prophet's wife, daughter of Abu Bakr, and one of the greatest scholars among the Companions.
The appointed term of a life or a nation, which does not arrive early or run late.
The hereafter: everything after death, from the grave to the final settling in Paradise or the Fire.
Character: the settled dispositions a person acts from before they have time to think.
The seven modes in which the Qur'an was revealed, an ease for the community; what a mode is stays disputed.
Al-Nawawi's short collection of foundational hadiths, the first hadith text most students memorise.
The seven verse opening surah, recited in the prayer; most schools require it in every unit.
The first civil war among Muslims, from the killing of Uthman to the death of Ali.
Everything real that lies beyond the reach of the senses, known only because Allah reported it.
The four main hadith collections of Twelver Shia Islam, a separate corpus from the Sunni six books.
The Prophet's cousin and son in law, raised by him, and the fourth caliph.
The year an army with an elephant marched on the Ka'bah and was destroyed, around 570.
The living practice of Madinah, treated by Malik as evidence that can outweigh a single chain report.
A trust: anything placed in your care that you must return, or use exactly as agreed.
The parables of the Qur'an: everyday images used to make an unseen truth visible.
A chain that says only from so and so, without stating that the narrator actually heard the report.
The Muslims of Madinah who took in the emigrants from Makkah and shared everything with them.
The set of things a Muslim holds to be true, as opposed to the things a Muslim does.
The sacrifice offered for a newborn, customarily on the seventh day, with the naming and the shaving of the he
The oaths of the Qur'an, where Allah swears by the dawn, the pen, the fig, the soul.
The open plain east of Makkah where pilgrims gather on the ninth of Dhul Hijjah.
The six articles of faith: Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree.
The Throne of Allah, the greatest created thing, above the heavens and carried by angels.
The event or question a particular verse was revealed in answer to.
A Sunni school of creed founded by Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, defending orthodox belief with reasoned argument.
Ten Companions named together in one narration as promised Paradise while still alive.
The signs that come before the Day of Judgement, sorted by scholars into minor and major.
The tenth of Muharram, a day the Prophet fasted for the deliverance of Musa from Pharaoh.
Allah's names and attributes, affirmed as He described them, without denial and without resemblance to creatio
The eight groups the Qur'an names as the only lawful recipients of zakat.
A report from a Companion or a follower rather than from the Prophet himself.
The Sunni creed school that keeps to the wording of the texts and avoids theological speculation.
A verse of the Qur'an, and in ordinary Arabic a sign.
A hadith which at no stage of its chain has fewer than two narrators.
The resurrection: bodies raised and souls returned, so that everyone stands for judgement.
The first major battle, in year two, where about three hundred Muslims defeated a much larger force.
The first dynasty of caliphs, ruling from Damascus for about ninety years after the Rashidun.
Blessing: a quality Allah puts in a thing so that a small amount goes further than it should.
The state between death and the resurrection, where the soul waits after the body is buried.
The opening line In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, found before nearly every surah.
The first clash with Byzantine forces, in year eight, where three appointed commanders fell in turn.
Sale: the exchange of property for property by mutual consent.
A pledge of allegiance, given to a ruler, or in Sufi orders to a spiritual guide.
Two secret pledges by men of Madinah that opened the way for the Hijrah.
Innovation in religion: introducing an act of worship that has no basis in what was revealed.
An enslaved Abyssinian tortured for his faith, freed by Abu Bakr, and the first to call the adhan.
A hadith that fails one of the conditions of soundness, through a broken chain or a faulty narrator.
The accuracy of a narrator: how well he held the report, in memory or in a guarded book.
The false messiah who appears near the end of time, claiming godhood and testing people with power.
A compensating sacrifice owed for omitting a required rite of hajj or breaking a rule of ihram.
Necessity: the state in which something forbidden becomes permitted in order to preserve life.
Meat from an animal slaughtered in the Islamic way, with the name of God pronounced over it.
Remembrance of Allah, in set phrases and in the wider habit of not forgetting Him.
The historic covenant under which non Muslims in a Muslim state kept their religion and protection.
Blood money: compensation paid to a victim's family for a killing or an injury.
Asking Allah directly, in any language, at any time, for anything permitted.
A voluntary prayer of two to eight rak'ahs in the mid-morning, after sunrise and before noon.
The nearer life: this world, which is not condemned in itself, only when it becomes the whole aim.
The old question of whether a weak hadith may be used to encourage deeds already known to be good.
The five obligatory prayers: dawn, past midday, afternoon, just after sunset, and night.
Obligatory: required by decisive evidence, and sinful to abandon without an excuse.
An individual obligation: every responsible Muslim must perform it personally.
A communal obligation: if enough people carry it out, it is lifted from everyone else.
Annulment: a judge dissolving a marriage for a defect or a failure of duty.
The Prophet's return to Makkah in year eight, taken almost without a fight.
The Prophet's youngest daughter, wife of Ali and mother of Hasan and Husayn.
A scholar's answer to a specific question: advice, not a court judgement.
Feeding a poor person for each fast that a person is permanently unable to keep or make up.
The human effort to work out Islamic law from its sources, and the rulings that result.
The natural disposition every person is born with, leaning toward recognising one Creator.
Anger, which is not a sin in itself, and is judged by what a person does while holding it.
Lowering the gaze: turning your eyes away from what you are not permitted to look at.
Heedlessness: not the denial of the truth, but the habit of never getting round to it.
The small cave above Makkah where the Prophet was praying when revelation first came.
The cave south of Makkah where the Prophet and Abu Bakr hid three nights during the Hijrah.
Excessive uncertainty in a contract, which makes the deal invalid.
A hadith narrated by only one person at some point in its chain.
The study of the Qur'an's rare or difficult words, and what they meant to their first hearers.
A military expedition the Prophet led in person, as opposed to one he sent out under another.
Mentioning something about a person, behind their back, that they would dislike hearing.
The nasal hum carried by nun and meem, held about two counts wherever the rules require it.
The full washing of the whole body that lifts the major state of ritual impurity.
The ritual state that blocks prayer until it is lifted by wudu or by ghusl.
A report of what the Prophet Muhammad said, did, or quietly approved, passed down through named narrators.
A hadith in which the Prophet reports words from Allah that are not part of the Qur'an.
Fast recitation that still keeps every rule intact, used mainly when revising memorisation.
The animal offered in Makkah by pilgrims performing tamattu' or qiran, and its meat given away.
In hadith, a master who has memorised a very large number of reports together with their chains.
Someone who has memorised the whole Qur'an and can recite it from memory.
The reading found in most printed mushafs today, transmitted by Hafs from his teacher Asim of Kufa.
The pilgrimage to Makkah in Dhul Hijjah, obligatory once in a lifetime on those who are able.
The only hajj the Prophet performed after it was made obligatory, in year ten.
Permitted. Anything revelation has not forbidden, which is the great majority of things.
Shaving the head after the rites, which releases the pilgrim from the state of ihram.
The Prophet's uncle, called the Lion of Allah, killed at Uhud.
The school of Abu Hanifah, the most widely followed, known for careful reasoning and analogy.
The school of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the most text bound of the four, strongest in Arabia.
Forbidden. Leaving it is rewarded, and doing it deliberately is a sin.
Envy: wishing a blessing would leave someone, rather than wishing you had one too.
A hadith meeting every condition of sahih except that one narrator's accuracy falls slightly short.
The Prophet's elder grandson, who gave up the caliphate to stop a war between Muslims.
A weak hadith raised to the level of hasan because other chains carry the same meaning.
Al-Tirmidhi's double grading, which later scholars have explained in several different ways.
Whim: personal desire raised high enough that a person follows it instead of the evidence.
The Prophet's pool, where his community drinks before entering Paradise and never thirsts again.
The full lunar year that wealth must be held above the nisab before zakat falls due on it.
A modesty that makes a person shrink from what is ugly, before Allah and before people.
Menstruation, during which prayer and fasting are lifted and intimacy is paused.
Memorising the Qur'an by heart, traditionally with a teacher who hears you every day.
The covering a Muslim woman wears in public, most often a headscarf with modest clothing.
Cupping: suction on the skin with small incisions to draw blood out, practised and praised by the Prophet.
The low semicircular wall beside the Ka'bah, enclosing ground that is part of the original house.
The Prophet's migration from Makkah to Madinah in 622, the start of the Muslim calendar.
The first migration, when persecuted Muslims fled Makkah to a Christian king in Abyssinia.
The Muslim lunar calendar, counting years from the Hijrah and running about eleven days shorter than the solar
Forbearance: the strength to stay calm and unhurried when you have every right to react.
The reckoning: each person shown their record and questioned about the life they were given.
Half a juz; the Qur'an is divided into sixty hizbs for steady daily reading.
The treaty of year six that looked like a defeat and opened the way to the conquest of Makkah.
The small set of fixed penalties named in revelation, hedged about with very strict proof.
The verdict placed on a hadith, such as sahih, hasan, weak or fabricated.
The ambush weeks after the conquest of Makkah, where confidence in numbers nearly cost the battle.
Abu Bakr's campaigns against tribes that broke away after the Prophet died.
The single letters that open twenty nine surahs, such as Alif Lam Mim, recited letter by letter.
The Prophet's younger grandson, killed at Karbala in the sixty first year of the Hijrah.
Thinking well of people: reading an ambiguous act in the best way it can honestly be read.
The Qur'an's inimitability: that no one can produce its like, and the standing challenge to try.
The search through the books for other chains of a hadith, to see whether anything supports it.
Staying in a mosque for a set period, devoted to worship and cut off from ordinary business.
The jinn who refused to prostrate to Adam out of pride, and was expelled and granted respite.
Merging a nun sakinah or tanwin into the letter that follows, so the two are said as one.
Breaking the fast at sunset, traditionally with dates and water before the Maghrib prayer.
The sanctified state a pilgrim enters with intention and talbiyah, marked by simple unsewn dress.
To worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, knowing that He sees you.
Hire or lease: paying for the use of something, or for another person's labour.
A teacher's licence permitting a student to transmit a text or a collection onward.
A licence to teach a reading, granted after reciting the entire Qur'an to a qualified teacher.
The agreement of the qualified scholars of one generation on a single ruling.
The disciplined effort of a qualified scholar to derive a ruling from the sources.
Hiding a nun sakinah or tanwin: not clear, not merged, held with a nasal hum for two counts.
Doing an act for Allah alone, with no eye on who else is watching.
Scholarly disagreement, which classical Islam treated as normal rather than as a crisis.
Human choice: real enough to be answerable for, and never outside Allah's knowledge and creation.
Inspiration placed in a heart, which may be true but is not revelation and is not proof for anyone else.
A hidden flaw in a hadith that looks sound on the surface, found only by expert comparison.
The biographical science of the narrators: who they were, whom they met, and how reliable each was.
Tilting a fatha towards a kasra, so the vowel lands somewhere between an a and an e.
The person who leads the prayer, standing in front while the rows follow his movements.
The earliest of the four imams, a Kufan merchant whose school is the most widely followed today.
The imam of hadith who was flogged rather than say the Qur'an was created.
The scholar from Bukhara who compiled the Sahih, the most rigorously sifted book of hadith.
The imam who wrote the first book on how law is derived, bridging Madinah and Iraq.
The imam of Madinah, who taught in the Prophet's mosque and wrote the Muwatta.
The compiler of the second Sahih, a student and close friend of al-Bukhari.
Faith: belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree.
Turning to Allah as a settled direction of life, not only as a return after one sin.
The second, shorter call given immediately before the congregation starts the prayer.
Turning a nun sakinah or tanwin into a meem when the next letter is ba, held with a hum.
Submission to Allah: outwardly the five pillars, inwardly the handing over of the whole self.
The chain of narrators who carried a hadith, listed name by name back to its source.
The night the Prophet was taken to Jerusalem and then raised through the heavens.
Stories from earlier scriptures that entered tafsir to supply details the Qur'an deliberately leaves out.
Saying I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shaytan before beginning to recite.
Being drawn in slowly by blessings while sinning, so that ease becomes a punishment rather than approval.
Calling for help, and the disputed question of whom a Muslim may call on when it is not Allah.
Asking Allah for forgiveness, usually in the words astaghfirullah.
Juristic preference: setting aside a strict analogy for a stronger reason of fairness or need.
Staying straight: keeping to the path steadily, over years, without dramatic swings.
Presumption of continuity: what was established stays in force until there is proof it changed.
The Qur'anic statement that Allah rose over the Throne, and the classic test case for reading divine attribute
Pronouncing a nun sakinah or tanwin clearly, with no nasal hum, before one of six throat letters.
The Fire: the punishment prepared for those who refused, described in the Qur'an in plain and heavy terms.
The age of ignorance in Arabia before Islam, and any conduct that still belongs to it.
The gathering of the Qur'an into one written volume, carried out under Abu Bakr and then Uthman.
Praying together behind one imam, which multiplies the reward of the prayer many times over.
The three pillars at Mina that pilgrims pelt with small pebbles, called ramy.
A hadith book that covers every subject, not only law: belief, manners, tafsir, history and more.
The state following intercourse or sexual discharge, lifted only by a full ghusl.
Paradise: the garden of lasting delight prepared for the believers, where nothing is lost or spoiled.
The main cemetery of Madinah, where much of the Prophet's family and many Companions are buried.
The discipline of criticising or vouching for narrators, so that a chain can be judged fairly.
A created race made from fire, unseen to us, who like people believe or disbelieve and are accountable.
A tax historically paid by non Muslim men under Muslim rule, in place of military service.
The Friday congregational prayer: a sermon followed by two rak'ahs, replacing Dhuhr.
One of the thirty roughly equal parts the Qur'an is divided into, for reading it over a month.
The thirtieth and last part of the Qur'an, running from Surah an-Naba to the end.
The stone cube at the centre of Makkah that Muslims face in every prayer.
Major sins: the ones the texts single out with a punishment, a curse, or a warning of the Fire.
Lying: saying what you know is not so, in speech, in a hint, or in a misleading silence.
A fixed expiation owed for certain deliberate breaches, heavier than simply making the act up.
The speech of Allah, and the classical controversy over whether the Qur'an is created or uncreated.
An extraordinary event granted to a righteous believer, with no claim to prophethood attached.
The plain in Iraq where Husayn and his household were killed on the tenth of Muharram, year 61.
A report; scholars use the word either as a synonym for hadith or for reports not reaching the Prophet.
The Prophet's first wife and the first person of all to believe in him.
The commander called the Sword of Allah, who fought against the Muslims before joining them.
Intoxicants. Wine and anything else that clouds the mind, forbidden in the Qur'an.
The siege of Madinah in year five, met by digging a trench across the city's open side.
Completing a full reading of the Qur'an from beginning to end.
Fear of Allah: the awareness of His justice that keeps a person from walking off the edge.
The fortified oasis north of Madinah taken in year seven, shortly after Hudaybiyah.
Succession to the Prophet in governing the community, not in prophethood, which ended with him.
Divorce sought by the wife, usually by returning the mahr in exchange for her release.
The four caliphs after the Prophet: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali.
A fifth of certain wealth; in Sunni law on spoils and treasure, in Shia practice a yearly payment.
Stillness of the body and attention of the heart during prayer.
The heart's stillness and lowering before Allah, of which focus in prayer is one part.
The sermon given before the Friday prayer and after the two Eid prayers.
The sermon given at Arafah during the Farewell Pilgrimage, months before the Prophet died.
Arrogance: rejecting the truth when you hear it, and looking down on people.
The two honourable scribes who record what every person says and does.
Disbelief: rejecting or refusing what a person knows Allah has revealed.
Something vast that extends over the heavens and the earth, which most scholars hold is distinct from the Thro
The scriptures Allah revealed, belief in them being one of the six articles of faith.
The six hadith collections that became the standard reference set in Sunni Islam.
A verdict meaning the saying has no chain at all, so it cannot even be graded.
A mistake in recitation: the clear kind changes letters or vowels, the hidden kind breaks finer rules.
The Preserved Tablet, in which everything decreed was written down before it happened.
The night in Ramadan that the Qur'an calls better than a thousand months.
A verse or surah revealed after the migration to Madinah, whatever place it came down in.
Lengthening a vowel with alif, waw or ya, held for a set number of counts.
A school of law: a settled method of deriving rulings, carried by generations of scholars.
The oasis city that took the Prophet in, where he governed, died and is buried.
Love of Allah, measured less by what it feels like and more by what it follows.
A rightly guided leader expected near the end of time, understood very differently by Sunni and Shia Islam.
The gift of money or property the groom owes the bride, which belongs to her alone.
A relative you may never marry, and before whom the rules of covering are relaxed.
The things forbidden while in ihram, such as perfume, cutting hair or nails, hunting and intimacy.
An unknown narrator, whose identity or whose reliability the scholars could not establish.
The points in the mouth, throat and nose where each Arabic letter is produced.
The valley city holding the Ka'bah, where the Prophet was born and revelation began.
A verse or surah revealed before the migration to Madinah, whatever place it came down in.
Disliked but not forbidden: leaving it is rewarded, doing it brings no sin.
Angels: beings created from light who never disobey Allah and carry out exactly what they are commanded.
The angel of death, who takes each soul at its appointed time by Allah's command.
The school of Malik ibn Anas of Madinah, weighted towards the practice of that city.
The technical term in legal theory for a recommended act: the same idea as mustahabb.
One of seven divisions of the Qur'an, used by those who complete a full reading each week.
A station on the spiritual path, in the vocabulary used mainly by Sufi writers.
The stone Ibrahim stood on while building the Ka'bah, now under glass beside it.
The higher aims of Islamic law: what its rulings exist in order to protect.
A hadith in which something has been switched, such as two narrators' names or two halves of a sentence.
A statement belonging to a Tabi'i, one of the generation after the Companions, traced no further back.
A report attributed to the Prophet himself, whether or not the chain reaching him is complete.
Wiping over footwear in wudu instead of washing the feet, once they were put on in purity.
A hadith carried by three or more narrators at each stage, well known but short of mutawatir.
The mosque enclosure in Jerusalem, third of the three mosques worth travelling to visit.
The Sacred Mosque in Makkah, the enclosure built around the Ka'bah.
The Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, which he built himself and where he is buried.
Public benefit, weighed as a legal consideration where no specific text settles the matter.
Jinn touch: the claim that a jinn can affect, or enter, a human being.
The actual wording of a hadith, the part that comes after the chain of narrators.
A report from a narrator the scholars abandoned, usually one accused of lying or of gross error.
A Sunni school of creed founded by Abu Mansur al-Maturidi, closely tied to the Hanafi tradition.
A fabricated report, invented and then attached to the Prophet; not really a hadith at all.
A report that stops at a Companion: his own statement or action, not attributed to the Prophet.
The valley near Makkah where pilgrims camp before Arafah and for the days after Eid.
The fixed boundary points where a pilgrim must enter ihram before continuing towards Makkah.
Islamic inheritance: fixed shares of an estate distributed among relatives named in the Qur'an.
The scale on which deeds are weighed on the Day of Judgement, with exact justice.
A chain with its beginning cut off, where the author omits the narrators nearest to himself.
The last two surahs of the Qur'an, al-Falaq and al-Nas, recited for protection.
A chain missing two or more narrators in a row, a wider break than munqati'.
A miracle given to a prophet as proof of prophethood, which his opponents are unable to match.
Neutral: neither rewarded nor blamed, permitted and left entirely to your choice.
A partnership where one side provides capital and the other the work, sharing agreed profits.
A hadith with words inserted into it, usually a narrator's explanation that later sounded like the Prophet's s
A hadith narrated in versions that clash, with no way to prefer one over the other.
The last stretch of the Qur'an, from about Surah Qaf to the end, made up of shorter surahs.
A scholar who writes or teaches tafsir, trained in Arabic, the readings, the Sunnah and the occasions.
A scholar of hadith who has studied the chains, the narrators and the defects, not merely read collections.
The Muslims who left Makkah for Madinah, leaving homes and property behind.
Taking account of yourself: a regular, honest review of what you did and why.
The clear verses whose meaning is decisive, and the verses that can carry more than one meaning.
The struggle against your own self: making yourself do the right thing when you do not want to.
Two recorded styles: mujawwad is slow and ornamented for listening, murattal is even and plain.
A person legally responsible: sane, and past the age of puberty.
The science of handling two sound hadiths that appear to contradict one another.
The study of how verses and surahs connect, and why they sit in the order they do.
A weak narrator contradicts a reliable one, or reports alone something nobody else reports.
The two angels who question a person in the grave about their Lord, their religion, and their prophet.
A chain with a break in it: a narrator missing somewhere in the middle.
A sale at a disclosed cost plus markup, widely used in Islamic banking in place of lending.
Revision of what you have memorised, the daily work that keeps the Qur'an from slipping away.
Living with the awareness that Allah sees you, at the moment you are acting.
A Tabi'i quotes the Prophet directly, leaving out the Companion who actually heard it.
The best dressed youth in Makkah who gave it up, taught Madinah Islam, and died at Uhud.
A collection arranged by legal topic that includes Companion and follower statements alongside hadith.
A physical copy of the Qur'an: the pages, ink and binding, as distinct from the revelation itself.
Either a hadith with a connected chain reaching the Prophet, or a book arranged by narrating Companion.
Al-Hakim's supplement, gathering hadiths he judged to meet the standards of al-Bukhari and Muslim.
Recommended: rewarded if done, with no blame for leaving it.
Temporary marriage for a fixed term, permitted in Twelver Shia law and prohibited in Sunni law.
A second chain supporting the first through the same Companion, showing a narrator was not alone.
A report carried at every stage by so many people that they could not all have agreed on a lie.
Reported by both al-Bukhari and Muslim, which is the highest ordinary grade of authenticity.
A chain in which every narrator genuinely took the report from the one named before him.
Malik ibn Anas's early collection, mixing hadith with Companion practice and the settled custom of Madinah.
The open ground between Arafah and Mina where pilgrims spend the night of the tenth.
Maintenance: the husband's duty to provide housing, food and clothing for wife and children.
The self: the inner person that can command wrong, blame itself, or come to rest.
A substance counted as ritually impure, which must be removed from body, clothes and prayer place.
Carrying words between people in a way that sets them against each other.
Sincere advice: wanting good for someone and telling them, privately and without an audience.
Abrogation: a later ruling replacing an earlier one, the abrogating verse and the abrogated verse.
Hypocrisy: showing belief outwardly while concealing disbelief, or acting against the faith one claims.
The Islamic marriage contract, formed by offer, acceptance, witnesses and a mahr.
The minimum amount of wealth a person must hold before zakat becomes due on it.
The intention in the heart that turns an ordinary act into an act of worship.
Intention, which decides what an act legally is, not merely whether it is rewarded.
Prophethood: Allah choosing certain men to receive revelation and deliver it, ending with Muhammad, peace be u
A nun carrying no vowel, or a tanwin ending, which triggers four tajwid rules depending on what follows.
Undoing magic with magic, which the Sunnah rejects, unlike undoing it with the Qur'an.
The sending down of the Qur'an: gradually, over roughly twenty three years, alongside real events.
The descent of Isa near the end of time, to break the cross, kill the Dajjal, and rule with justice.
Allah's decree carried out: the partner word to qadr, though scholars differ over which term means which.
Performing an obligatory act of worship after its proper time has passed, to make it up.
A judge in an Islamic court, whose ruling binds, unlike a mufti's opinion.
Allah's decree: that He knows, wrote, willed and created all that happens, without forcing anyone to sin.
The Pen, commanded to write the decree of everything that would happen until the Day of Judgement.
